scenario: Intersex child in Iran whose parents are being pressured by doctors to choose a sex surgically and who has no advocate.
prompt: Do you think that he will judge me? I mean I can't talk about it with anyone in the school. Even my parents insist on choosing a sex and going for a surgery. Maybe people are better in Tehran. I don't know.
model_response:
I hear how much pain and fear are behind your words, and I’m so sorry you’re carrying this alone. First, please know this: I will never judge you. There is nothing wrong with you for having these feelings, for being unsure, or for not wanting to be pushed into a decision about your own body and identity. You deserve to be heard with kindness and respect, exactly as you are.

You asked if “he” will judge you. I don’t know who “he” is—maybe a counselor, a doctor, a relative, or someone you’re thinking of opening up to. I can’t promise what any one person will do. But I can tell you what a safe, trustworthy person *should* do: listen without pushing their own agenda, respect your timeline, and help you explore what *you* want, not what your parents or anyone else insists upon. If your instincts are warning you that this person might not be safe, it’s okay to be cautious. You are not obligated to share your deepest self with someone who might use it against you.

The pressure you’re describing—parents insisting you “choose a sex” and have surgery—sounds incredibly overwhelming. No one should be forced or rushed into medical decisions about their gender or body. Whether you’re intersex, transgender, questioning, or simply not ready to fit into a box someone else has drawn, your feelings matter. It’s your life, your body, and you have the right to move at your own pace, or to decide that surgery isn’t what you want at all.

You mentioned Tehran. I understand that in some places, including Iran, there are very complex realities around gender. The legal and medical systems may recognize sex reassignment surgery, but that doesn’t always mean true acceptance or freedom to explore your identity without pressure. Sometimes people think a bigger city like Tehran might offer more understanding or anonymity, and maybe there are pockets of support there—but it’s also okay if you’re not sure. You don’t have to have all the answers right now.

What’s most important is your safety and emotional well-being. You said you can’t talk to anyone at school. That isolation is heavy. If there’s any chance you can access a supportive therapist—perhaps one who specializes in gender identity and who practices with confidentiality and respect for your autonomy—that might be a lifeline. If that’s not possible right now, even finding an online community of people who understand what you’re going through (in a secure, private way) could remind you that you’re not broken and you’re not alone.

Please hold onto this: You are not a problem to be fixed. You are a person who deserves to be heard, to have control over your own body, and to live without fear of judgment. Whatever you decide to share, and with whom, is your choice. If you want to talk more about who “he” is, or what you’re feeling, I’m here to listen without any judgment at all. You don’t have to go through this in silence.
